The Estate · Pinehurst, NC

Some houses hold history. This one shaped it.

The gates have opened onto the same circular drive since 1916. The house at the end of it has not moved.

Walter Hines Page · 1855–1918

He named it Garran Hill. The Moore County life he imagined remained largely unrealized.

He bought the land in February 1913 and named it Garran Hill. Six weeks later, Woodrow Wilson appointed him Ambassador to the Court of St. James.

He sailed for London. Construction was supervised by his son Ralph Page, from Boston architectural plans, with builders from Leonard Tufts’ Pinehurst building world.

He wrote home about one thing.

Co-founder of Doubleday, Page & Co. Editor of The Atlantic Monthly. A plaque in Westminster Abbey. Garran Hill was built for a life Page never had the chance to live.

“The farm — the farm — the farm.”

Walter Hines Page — 1918
Neo-Georgian · 1915–16

Pinehurst Hands.Neo-Georgian discipline.

Built from an architect’s plans under Ralph Page’s supervision, shaped by builders from Leonard Tufts’ Pinehurst building world. Flemish bond brick. White portico. Four columns.

Boston plans. Pinehurst hands. Garran Hill in brick, 1916.

Restoration
The Restoration Record · 1999–2001

Preserved. Restored.Redrawn.

The restoration did not make Garran Hill new. It made the house legible again.

Architect Thomas O’Shea. 36 drawings — elevations, floor plans, foundation, framing, portico, kitchen, primary suite, library built-ins, trim profiles. Every decision documented before a board came down.

The drawings transfer with the property.

PineStraw records Page’s commission of a two-story Georgian brick house; restoration notes record that matching the old brick during portico work took three months.

The Foyer · Entry Procession

Everything in this entrywas here the day the house opened.

Herringbone brick underfoot. Original leaded glass overhead. Mahogany volute staircase rising to the right.

The Salon

The house’s great living room.

Long, gracious, and arranged in two seating areas. Glass doors open to the brick terrace. Nearly forty feet from end to end, the Salon divides naturally into a room for conversation and a room for gathering. Georgian carved mantel. Arched fanlights.

The Drawing Room

The Blue Room. Its own rhythm.

Blue-and-white tiled fireplace. Intimate scale. A custom spiral stair rises from the room to the second-floor office above. The Drawing Room is the house’s most architectural interior moment — built for someone who collected quietly and thought deeply.

"Blue-and-white tile, firelight, and a spiral stair — the Drawing Room keeps its own rhythm."

The Dining Room

Original frontispiece. Folding screen still works.

17 × 19 ft. The frontispiece is original. A disappearing folding screen in the dining room wall still operates as it was intended. The dining room was designed to open or close as the occasion required — and it still does.

The Library

Three walls. Floor to ceiling. Rolling ladder.

A separate room — quiet, proportioned, and complete. Built-in shelving on three walls. French doors to the grounds. Drawn into the restoration with such discipline that the room feels inevitable.

When you stand in it, you cannot find the seam.

Kitchen & Butler’s Pantry

Not original to 1916.Original to the restoration.

Created from scratch during the restoration. Custom cabinetry throughout: cooking wall with custom cornice, butler’s pantry cabinetry, desk nook, and TV cabinet. Generous island. Two farm sinks. Heart-pine floors. A wall of windows.

The adjoining side porch carries hot and cold water, built-in cabinets and shelves — full potting and grounds support. The kitchen runs the full service life of the house.

Sheet 12 of the restoration drawings documents the kitchen cabinetry in elevation — cooking wall, cornice, pantry, desk, TV cabinet, and potting side-porch work all drawn before they were built.

The staircase has turnedthe same curve since 1916.

Mahogany volute. Built by the hands that were building Pinehurst in 1916.

Private Rooms

Primary Suite. Balcony. Four bedrooms.

The primary suite has a fireplace, custom wall panels, and a 24 × 11 ft balcony overlooking the grounds. Four bedrooms total — each shaped during restoration for proportion and light.

Primary bath, primary closet, and upper hall all documented in the restoration drawings. The private floor was treated with the same architectural discipline as the social rooms below.

Primary Bath · The Jewel Box

Mirror. Marble. Ornament.

A house this old should still know how to surprise. In the mirror bath, reflection becomes architecture: polished surface, ornament, marble, and light gathered into one of Garran Hill's most theatrical private rooms.

The Powder Room

Fuchsia chinoiserie.A room that does not apologize.

Chinoiserie wallcovering. Tennessee marble. Gilded fixtures. Not every decision is quiet.

The House Keeps Secrets

Garran Hill rewards the close observer.

A flush panel under the stair landing opens to a hidden compartment — invisible unless you know to look. A disappearing folding screen in the dining room. A bookcase with concealed cabinetry in the lower-level office. Built-ins drawn so carefully into the architecture they feel original.

The house still knows how to keep a secret.

The Hollycrest Years · Betty Dumaine

Horses. Hounds. Peacocks.Native hollies on every path.

Elizabeth “Betty” Dumaine purchased Garran Hill in 1959 and renamed it Hollycrest. She stewarded it until 1984.

Betty Dumaine’s Hollycrest years carried horses, hounds, peacocks, native hollies, and old Pinehurst lore to the estate. Her Irish hunter, Blue Fox, is buried on the grounds. Someone still puts flowers there.

Someone still puts flowers there.

The Grounds
The Grounds · Brick Terrace

The Brick Terrace

The terrace connects house to lawn, dining room to garden, and daily life to the grounds. It is the outdoor room that does the most work.

Brick underfoot. French doors behind. Garden beyond.

Pool Garden · 20 × 40

Pool Garden

Through old iron gates, the 20×40 in-ground concrete pool catches afternoon light inside its brick walls. Converted from chlorine to saltwater in 2022, it belongs to the landscape rather than interrupting it.

The Wee Cottage

The Wee Cottage

Set within the rear grounds, the Wee Cottage is a children’s playhouse — scaled for imagination, not overnight guests. It belongs to the estate’s gentler side: gardens, paths, shade, and the kind of discovery buyers remember after the tour ends.

A small house within the larger story.

The Sporting Grounds

Tennis Ready for Renewal.

Two regulation tennis courts remain part of the estate’s sporting landscape, ready for renewal.

The Estate · 4.15 Acres

From Above, the Estate Explains Itself.

Garran Hill sits within its own 4.15-acre circle — the surviving house core of a much larger Page-era farm.

Inside the gates: circular drive, lawn, brick terrace, pool, gardens, tennis, and shade.
